title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for Steiner Tree
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\), the infimum of achievable expected polynomial-time approximation ratios for the undirected weighted Steiner Tree problem.
definitions: An instance is a finite connected undirected simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), an explicitly listed terminal subset \(R\subseteq V\) with \(|R|\ge2\), and nonnegative rational edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). A solution is a tree subgraph containing every vertex in R and any subset of the other vertices. Its cost is the sum of its edge weights, and OPT is the minimum such cost. The graph is represented by its complete vertex and edge lists. There are no restrictions on graph topology, terminal count, or weight magnitudes. An algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine with independent fair random bits. Its worst-case running time, over all random tapes, is polynomial in the binary input length. It always returns a feasible solution, and its expected cost is measured over its coins. A real number \(r\ge1\) is achievable if one such algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}(A(I))]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every valid instance I. The target is the infimum of achievable r; the polynomial and algorithm may depend on r. An infimum need not be attained. All integers and rational input data use explicit binary encodings, with numerator and positive denominator for each rational; their full lengths count toward the input size. No complexity assumption is built into the definition. Instances with OPT=0 are included and require zero expected output cost.

context_blocks.text: Steiner vertices may reduce the cost of connecting the required terminals. Requiring all terminals in a single connected tree distinguishes this target from Steiner Forest, while undirected edges distinguish it from Directed Steiner Tree.
The ln 4 approximation was established through randomized rounding and recovered by a later combinatorial approach. These results do not identify the best possible polynomial-time ratio.

why: Determine the efficient-approximation limit of the basic network-design problem that underlies many more general connectivity objectives.

progress.text: Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoss and Sanita obtain ratios approaching ln 4.
Traub and Zenklusen recover the ln 4 guarantee through a combinatorial approach.

answer_criterion: Supply a real number a and a complete Lean-checked proof that its absolute difference from the defined constant is at most \(1/100\). A proved containing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. The constant is unconditional: a lower bound relying on an unproved complexity assumption settles only the corresponding conditional statement. Merely restating the defining infimum is not a determination.

sentences: Steiner Tree connects a specified terminal set using optional additional graph vertices.
The input graph and its nonnegative rational edge weights are unrestricted.
The card asks for the best expected approximation ratio among all uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms.
Different algorithmic approaches reach ln 4 without establishing the optimal threshold.
Benchmark acceptance requires a Lean-certified value within absolute error 0.01.
